ann_37.text: This part acts on 28 of 242 training patients (12%); 14 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, a resting blood pressure of 120 mm Hg, 1.9 mm of ST depression, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 91% to about 66% (on the training data only).

Through it, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL, a reversible thallium defect or higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) raise that patient's predicted risk from about 66% to about 91% (on the training data only).
A fixed thallium defect raises it from about 66% to about 77% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, 15 patients).
For patients with a reversible thallium defect, resting blood pressure adds to the predicted risk through this part only once it rises above about 109 mm Hg (on the training data only).
A downsloping ST segment changes it only slightly here (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, 17 patients).

ann_38.text: This part acts on 66 of 242 training patients (27%); 13 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 48-year-old man with non-anginal chest pain, a maximum heart rate of 172 beats per minute, a normal resting ECG and a normal thallium scan), it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 4% to about 2% (on the training data only).

summary.text: For a typical patient, number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy going from 0 vessels to 2 vessels raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 38% to about 93% (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, serum cholesterol going from 193 mg/dL (5.0 mmol/L) to 308 mg/dL (8.0 mmol/L) raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 25% to about 60% (on the training data only).
For a typical patient, the model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has typical angina (about 5%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 38%).

A higher ST depression on exercise clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL: for a typical patient, ST depression on exercise going from 0.0 mm to 2.8 mm moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 2% to about 66% if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL, and from about 38% to about 38% if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less.

The model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman than if the patient is a man if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less, but the other way if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL: for a typical patient, going from male to female moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 38% to about 3% if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less, and from about 2% to about 3% if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL.
